title: Follow a C return value
summary: Compile a trip charge locally and follow its returned value into a0.
objectives: Connect a C return expression with the register observed after a real function call.
Distinguish the C source from the compiler’s generated instruction sequence.
before: A compiler translates C into machine instructions. The editor now accepts a complete C function named `lesson`. TinyCC compiles it inside your browser into an object file: machine code whose address references still need resolving. The GNU linker joins that object with the supplied caller and reporting code, then resolves the addresses to make an executable for xv6. You can inspect the compiler’s output without sending your source to a compilation service.

The two arguments arrive in `a0` and `a1`. For the starting call, `a` is the trip distance and `b` is the charge per distance unit. The function first calculates their product in the local variable `charge`, then adds a fixed charge before returning. The supplied caller observes the return value in `a0`.

Both parameters and the return type are `unsigned long`. This target uses a 64-bit `unsigned long`, so its arithmetic keeps the low 64 bits. The function may change temporary registers while it works. The calling convention guarantees the result location; it does not promise that every incoming argument remains in its original register.

prediction.prompt: What unsigned value is in a0 when lesson(6, 4) returns?
prediction.hint: Work out the product assigned to charge, then add the constant in the return expression.

explanation: The name `charge` belongs to the C program. It does not attach a permanent type or name to a physical register. A compiler can keep a value in a register, place it on the stack, or replace it with another calculation that preserves the required result. After a successful build, open Inspect the real compiler output to see what TinyCC emitted.

A return statement provides the caller’s result. The compiler also emits the instructions needed to leave the function and restore any state it must preserve. One C expression can therefore correspond to several instructions. The disassembly is output from the current compilation, not a handwritten promise about how every compiler must implement the function.

Compiling successfully establishes that the tool accepted the source. Running one call checks that call. The exercise uses several fresh calls so a function that returns a fixed answer cannot satisfy the whole contract.

experiment.task: In the return expression, change charge + 7 to charge + 11. Predict the new return value, then choose Build & Run and inspect a0 in Registers.
experiment.hint: The product is unchanged. Follow only the constant added by the return expression.

challenge.task: Write an unsigned trip-charge function that returns a * b + 3 in a0. The two unsigned arguments arrive through the supplied caller. Keep unsigned 64-bit wrapping, including when the mathematical product is too large.
hints: Calculate the distance-dependent charge before adding the fixed charge.
Unsigned arithmetic wraps at the operation; a later addition uses the wrapped product.
The caller reads the function’s returned expression, not a local variable that was never returned.

originalityNote: The source course’s editable trip charge is compiled by the real browser TinyCC toolchain for RISC-V, with its ABI result captured after execution.

title: Choose a result in C
summary: Compile a limit check and test both paths of the returned result.
objectives: Follow the path selected by a signed C comparison.
Test a limit function below, at and above its boundaries.
before: An `if` statement chooses whether its body runs. The function below compares a measured value `a` with a limit `b`. If the measurement is greater, it returns the limit. Otherwise it returns the original measurement. This is a cap: it prevents the returned value from exceeding the limit.

The arguments and result use signed `long`, which is 64 bits on this target. A negative measurement therefore participates in a signed comparison. The result is observed in `a0` only after the selected path returns to the supplied caller. Neither path needs to execute the other path’s return statement.

A compiler can implement a C decision with more than one instruction sequence. After Build & Run, open Inspect the real compiler output to see TinyCC’s choice. RISC-V conditional branches compare register values directly; there is no separate Arm-style condition-flag register for the C expression to update.

prediction.prompt: What is in a0 after the capped measurement lesson(28, 20) returns?
prediction.hint: Evaluate a > b first. Use the return statement on that path; the other return does not run.

explanation: The comparison determines which value reaches the return location. It does not change the stored bits of the original measurement by itself. Follow the condition first, then the return statement on that path. Reading the listing from top to bottom without following a branch can make mutually exclusive operations look as though they both execute.

An upper cap is not a complete range check. A negative input is already below a non-negative limit, so the example leaves that negative value unchanged. If the application also requires a lower bound, it must express that requirement separately. Tests should cover both sides and equality, where neither a strict greater-than nor a strict less-than condition holds.

The challenge asks for a value in a closed range. It supplies only non-negative upper limits, keeping that contract consistent even when the measurement is negative. The function does not need a particular branch spelling to pass; it needs the correct returned value for every supplied call.

experiment.task: Before the if statement, add a = b; so this call compares equal values. Run once with > and once with >=. Compare a0 in Registers after each return. Explain whether the returned value alone tells you which return statement ran.
experiment.hint: Both runs compare equal values. Follow the condition to identify the return statement each run reaches.

challenge.task: Return a clamped measurement: return 0 when signed a is negative, return b when a exceeds b, and return a otherwise. The supplied upper limit b is always non-negative.
hints: An upper cap alone does not reject a negative measurement.
Check the lower boundary before returning the unchanged measurement.
Treat a value equal to a boundary as part of the allowed range.

originalityNote: The source course’s cap becomes a real RISC-V C compilation whose fresh exercise checks a lower boundary as well as an upper limit.

title: Compile a counted loop
summary: Connect a C loop’s test, body and update to a returned total.
objectives: Distinguish a loop’s test, body and update.
Check the zero-iteration case before relying on a counted loop.
before: A C `for` loop puts its initialisation, continuation test and update together. The initialisation runs once. Before each iteration, the continuation test decides whether the body runs. The update follows the body, then control returns to the test. The compiler must preserve this order for the defined calls used here.

The example starts `total` at zero and adds `b` once for each count below `a`. Both arguments are unsigned. With the supplied small count, the loop has a clear stopping point. The returned value is the total after the loop ends, not the value after the first addition.

The loop variable is a C value, not a promise to use one particular register. Build the current source, inspect its generated instructions, and find the comparison and backward control flow. The result cards capture the state after the whole function returns. They are not a recording of every intermediate iteration.

prediction.prompt: What unsigned total is returned after all iterations for a = 4 and b = 3?
prediction.hint: List the counter values that satisfy i < a. Each one adds b to the total, which starts at zero.

explanation: A zero count makes the continuation test false before the first body execution. Initialising the total before the loop therefore matters: the function still needs a result when it performs no additions. A test after the body would describe a different loop, with at least one body execution.

Changing `<` to `<=` changes the set of counts that reach the body. It can add an iteration even though the body is unchanged. Work out the first count, the last count that passes, and the update between them. This is more reliable than guessing the answer from the visual length of the loop.

These exercises restrict counts to at most 1000. That keeps the loop bounded well before its unsigned counter can wrap. Passing the supplied cases does not prove that an arbitrary loop terminates for every possible 64-bit input. Keep a bound or a progress argument with any repeated calculation.

experiment.task: In the for loop, change i < a to i <= a. Predict how many extra times the body runs for the starting count. Choose Build & Run and compare the returned total in a0 with the original run.
experiment.hint: The added path is the one where the counter equals the bound.

challenge.task: Return the sum of the integers from 1 through unsigned a, including a. The count a is between 0 and 1000; b is unused. A zero count must return zero.
hints: Name the first and last values that should be added.
The zero case must skip the body, leaving the initial total unchanged.
Starting at zero and stopping before a omits the last requested value.

originalityNote: The loop lesson retains test-before-body reasoning and adds a fresh inclusive-sum exercise executed by the actual RISC-V compiler/runtime.

title: Use a local array in C
summary: Compile array access and distinguish element offsets from byte offsets.
objectives: Relate a C array subscript to an element-sized address step.
Use defined unsigned arithmetic while reading a local array.
before: A local array groups several values of the same type inside a function. Its subscript selects an element: `samples[1]` is the second element, not the second byte. On this target a `long` occupies eight bytes. Earlier byte-addressed loads explain why neighbouring long elements need more than a one-byte address step.

The example gives three signed long elements their values from the two arguments and a fixed adjustment. It then returns their sum. Every subscript is within the declared three-element array, and the supplied inputs keep the signed addition within range. Observe `a0` after the function returns.

A pointer holds an address. For a pointer to long, adding one advances by one long element. C performs that scaling from the pointed-to type. The generated assembly has only addresses and instructions; it does not carry a C type label on each register. A compiler can also remove storage when an equivalent calculation preserves the required behaviour.

prediction.prompt: What is returned after the three initialised elements are added for a = 8 and b = -3?
prediction.hint: Follow the assignment to each samples element before adding them. An array subscript selects an element, not a byte.

explanation: The assignments give every element a value before this function reads it. Leaving an automatic local element uninitialised and then using its indeterminate value is not a sound way to create a test. The function also must not read beyond the array just because surrounding stack memory happens to be mapped.

The disassembly records this compiler’s implementation. You can look for frame-relative addresses and element loads if they are present, but the C source does not require a separate memory access for every written subscript. Do not infer an instruction count or a performance result from the source alone.

The exercise uses unsigned long elements so the requested weighted sum has defined 64-bit wrapping. The pointer must still stay within the two-element array. Arithmetic wrapping is a rule for integer values; it is not permission to form or dereference arbitrary addresses.

experiment.task: Change samples[2] = 2 to samples[2] = -2. Predict how the returned sum changes, then choose Build & Run and compare a0 in Registers. Keep every subscript inside the declared array.
experiment.hint: The first two elements still come from the same arguments; only the adjustment changes.

challenge.task: Create a two-element unsigned long array containing a and b. Use its elements to return a + 2*b with unsigned 64-bit arithmetic. Keep every access within those two elements.
hints: The second element contributes twice; the first contributes once.
A subscript counts elements of the pointed-to type, not raw bytes.
Unsigned arithmetic keeps the low 64 bits after the multiply and addition.

originalityNote: A short local array connects the existing byte-address lessons with real C compilation without inventing a permanent register allocation or memory trace.

title: Keep a type’s width separate from a register’s width
summary: Measure this C target’s integer sizes and test a defined narrowing conversion.
objectives: Distinguish a C type’s size from the 64-bit result register.
Apply unsigned byte conversion before widening the result.
before: `sizeof` gives a C type’s size in bytes. The expression below encodes two sizes into one returned number: the size of int contributes the hundreds, and the size of long contributes the units. This is a measurement of the selected compiler target. It is not a statement that the C language gives every machine those sizes.
The result register is 64 bits wide. That width does not tell you the C type sizes. Choose Build & Run with the expression unchanged, then read a0 in Registers to measure its size code.

A cast requests a conversion to a chosen type. Converting an integer to `unsigned char` keeps its value modulo 256 on this eight-bit-byte target. Returning that converted value as unsigned long then widens the value already obtained. Widening afterwards cannot recover high bits discarded by the earlier conversion.

prediction.prompt: You may leave the prediction blank and measure first. What code does 100*sizeof(int) + sizeof(long) return on this target?
prediction.hint: sizeof reports bytes, not bits. The result register’s width does not establish the sizes of the C types.

explanation: This lab uses the RV64 LP64 data model: int is 32 bits, while long and pointers are 64 bits. The result register’s width does not make an int operation into a long operation. A pointer and a long having the same size does not make them the same C type.

For the byte exercise, first perform the conversion to unsigned char, then read the returned widened value. A value just above the byte range does not remain just above the range. The conversion wraps within the destination type. If an application must reject that value instead, it must check the original input before narrowing.

Do not generalise the byte rule to an out-of-range conversion to signed char without checking the selected language version and implementation rules. This exercise deliberately uses unsigned char, where the conversion needed for its cases is defined. The unused second argument does not affect either measurement or conversion.

experiment.task: In the return expression, replace sizeof(long) with sizeof(void *), which asks for a pointer’s size. Predict whether the size code changes, then choose Build & Run and compare a0 in Registers.
experiment.hint: This target has 64-bit pointers as well as a 64-bit long; that equality is target-specific.

challenge.task: Convert unsigned argument a to unsigned char, then return that byte value widened to unsigned long. Argument b is unused. Do not reject out-of-range values; apply the defined unsigned conversion.
hints: The result must be within the unsigned-byte range.
The conversion happens before the return value is widened.
Returning a directly omits the narrowing operation, even though small inputs happen to pass.

originalityNote: The source course’s type-width and narrowing distinctions are measured on the real RV64 C target, avoiding Arm W-register zero-extension assumptions.

title: Separate C overflow from machine wrapping
summary: Run defined unsigned wrapping and protect a bounded increment before it wraps.
objectives: Explain why a machine’s wrapping addition does not define signed C overflow.
Check an input limit before computing a bounded increment.
before: An unsigned C addition has a defined wrapping result. For unsigned long on this target, it keeps the low 64 bits. The starting function adds the two supplied unsigned arguments. Its behaviour at the end of the unsigned range follows the C type’s rule as well as the instructions that implement it.

Signed C addition has a different contract. If the mathematical signed result is outside the signed type’s range, C describes the operation as undefined behaviour: the language places no requirements on that execution. It does not promise a wrapped value, an exception or an error message.

A RISC-V add instruction still has defined low-bit behaviour. That fact does not require a compiler to translate an overflowing signed C expression into that instruction. An optimiser can use the assumption that a defined signed addition does not overflow. This page’s executed cases use defined C; they do not treat one compiler’s response to undefined behaviour as a portable answer.

prediction.prompt: What unsigned value is returned when the largest unsigned long is increased by two?
prediction.hint: Form the unsigned sum, then keep only its low 64 bits. A carry beyond bit 63 is not stored.

explanation: Interpret the result in the type used by the source calculation. A signed decimal display can show a negative reading for a perfectly valid unsigned result whose top bit is set. The hexadecimal bits identify the same stored value without choosing a signed reading. A display choice does not change the C arithmetic that produced those bits.

If wrapping is unwanted, express a different application rule. A bounded increment can test whether the input is already the largest allowed value, then leave it unchanged. Testing first makes the rule explicit. Adding first and hoping a later comparison reconstructs an invalid signed operation does not repair undefined behaviour. In C, `0UL` is zero of type `unsigned long`. The `~` operator complements every bit, so `~0UL` is the largest unsigned long value.

Tests and compiler warnings help find mistakes, but neither proves that all possible inputs are safe. A run-time checker also observes only paths that execute. The exercise’s boundary cases make the intended behaviour visible without asking the browser compiler to diagnose every kind of C error.

experiment.task: Inside lesson, add a = 0; and b = 1; before the return statement. Change that statement to return a - b;. These assignments replace the supplied arguments within this call. Choose Build & Run and explain a0’s hexadecimal reading in Registers.
experiment.hint: Subtraction has the same unsigned modulo rule; the signed decimal reading is a separate choice.

challenge.task: Write an unsigned increment that stops at the largest unsigned long. Return a unchanged when it equals ~0UL; otherwise return a + 1. Argument b is unused.
hints: The largest unsigned long has every bit set.
Check that original input before deciding to perform the increment.
A wrapped zero is a defined arithmetic result, but it violates this exercise’s stop-at-the-limit rule.

originalityNote: The source course’s hardware-versus-C distinction is preserved while all live C cases remain defined and the exercise states an explicit unsigned boundary contract.

title: Check a sum before using it
summary: Turn a defined unsigned carry check into a saturating C addition.
objectives: Detect unsigned addition overflow from a defined wrapped sum.
Distinguish the stored sum from the decision about whether to use it.
before: A checked calculation returns or uses both a result and a decision about its range. The example forms an unsigned sum, then returns a Boolean: one when the mathematical sum does not fit, zero when it does. A Boolean result uses one for true and zero for false.

For unsigned addition, a wrapped sum is smaller than the first operand exactly when a carry was lost beyond the 64-bit result. The C comparison `sum < a` therefore checks this condition using defined unsigned operations. It is the same value relationship used by an explicit RISC-V unsigned comparison; no Arm-style carry flag is available.

The returned Boolean is not the sum. Observe the function’s return contract before interpreting a0. The challenge changes the contract to return a usable saturated sum: either the ordinary result or the largest unsigned long. The input types remain unsigned throughout, including the temporary variable.

prediction.prompt: What Boolean does the unsigned range check return for the largest unsigned long plus one?
prediction.hint: The function returns the comparison, not the sum. Compare the wrapped unsigned sum with the original a.

explanation: A range check answers whether the mathematical result fits the required destination. It does not make the wrapped bits into that mathematical result. Keep those two facts separate when choosing whether to store, reject, clamp or report a value. Different applications can use the same check and choose different policies.

This unsigned comparison must stay unsigned. Reinterpreting the sum as signed before testing changes which values are ordered below others. The top bit is part of the unsigned magnitude, not a negative sign for this calculation. A normal sum that sets that bit is not automatically an unsigned overflow.

Signed checking needs its own rule. In ordinary signed C, do not first calculate an overflowing signed sum to discover overflow afterwards. Check operands against valid bounds before adding, or use a checked-arithmetic facility supported by the chosen environment. The freestanding browser exercises do not provide a host checked-arithmetic library.

experiment.task: Before the sum assignment, add b = 0;. Predict the returned Boolean, then choose Build & Run and inspect a0. Next replace that line with a = 0x7fffffffffffffffUL; and b = 1;. Predict whether setting the sum’s top bit makes the range check true, then run again.
experiment.hint: These assignments change the arguments used inside the function. The returned Boolean checks a carry beyond bit 63, not the signed reading of the sum.

challenge.task: Return a saturated unsigned sum. Calculate a + b; if it overflows unsigned long, return ~0UL. Otherwise return the sum. Use only defined unsigned operations.
hints: Keep the wrapped sum in an unsigned local value.
Compare that sum with an original operand to detect the lost carry.
Return the maximum only for overflow; a sum equal to the maximum can still be a normal result.

originalityNote: The source course’s result-versus-overflow distinction becomes an explicit, fully defined unsigned C predicate rather than an Arm flag test.

title: Ask xv6 to write bytes
summary: Pass a byte range to xv6 and inspect the system call’s returned count.
objectives: Identify a system call’s number, arguments and return value.
Keep a byte count separate from a zero-terminated string length.
before: A user program asks the operating system to perform an operation with a system call. For xv6 write, a0 holds a file descriptor: a number naming an open file. a1 holds the first byte’s address, and a2 gives the byte count. The starter puts system call number 16 in a7 and executes ecall to ask xv6 to write.

The supplied program has file 1 open for standard output, the console used here. The example writes five bytes from lesson_data, then copies write’s returned value from a0 into t2. The snapshot is taken after that copy. The report is separate from the text that write sends to the console.

These numbers belong to xv6. Linux and teaching simulators can use different system call conventions even when they execute RISC-V instructions. `ecall` requests service from the execution environment; the instruction itself does not define what a file number or a write operation means.
starter:
li a0, 1
la a1, lesson_data
li a2, 5
li a7, 16
ecall
mv t2, a0

prediction.prompt: How many bytes does t2 report after the starting write succeeds?
prediction.hint: a2 supplies a byte count, not a zero-terminated string length. t2 receives the value returned in a0 after ecall.

explanation: Write uses the explicit count, not a search for a zero terminator. A zero byte inside the requested range is still one byte to write. Conversely, text beyond the requested range is not part of this request. A byte count also differs from a character count for text whose characters use more than one encoded byte.

The returned value reports the operation’s result. A successful xv6 write returns the bytes written; an error can return -1. The general purpose of checking the return is to distinguish an attempted operation from one that completed. The exercise keeps the file descriptor and source range valid so it can focus on the count.

The supplied reporting code also writes to the console after your fragment. That later write does not change the earlier snapshot of t2. Open Tools → Output. Program output shows your message bytes; xv6 serial log also includes the lab’s register report. No CPU flag announces that a system call succeeded.

experiment.task: Change li a2, 5 to li a2, 4. Predict the returned count, then choose Build & Run. Compare t2 in Registers and the message under Tools → Output → Program output. Which final message byte is no longer sent?
experiment.hint: The final byte is a newline. Omitting it affects presentation, not the number of earlier bytes requested.

challenge.task: Write exactly the unsigned byte count in t0 from the beginning of lesson_data to standard output. Counts are between 0 and 5, and those bytes are valid. Leave the returned write count in t2.
challenge.starter:
li a0, 1
la a1, lesson_data
li a2, 0
li a7, 16
ecall
mv t2, a0
challenge.reference:
li a0, 1
la a1, lesson_data
mv a2, t0
li a7, 16
ecall
mv t2, a0
hints: The count comes from the test input, not from a fixed number in the source.
Set the address and count before ecall; copy the result after it returns.
A zero count is still a valid request here and must report zero.

originalityNote: The source course’s real-output boundary is adapted to a user process’s xv6 write contract, keeping device access and Linux conventions out of the live example.

title: Follow the executable’s entry contract
summary: Connect a source fragment, a callable function and the complete ELF user program.
objectives: Distinguish a process entry from an ordinary function return.
Explain why editing source requires a fresh build and run.
before: An object file contains machine code and names that the linker still needs to resolve. The linker combines those contents, gives them addresses and writes an executable. This lab’s executable uses ELF, a file format whose headers describe the target, the entry address and the memory regions to load.

The program entry is where a newly started process begins. It is not an ordinary function called with a saved return address. The supplied _start code prepares the lesson’s inputs, runs your fragment, reports its results and asks xv6 to exit. Open View complete program to see that surrounding code.

Your fragment can still call an ordinary helper. The example calls advance and jumps past its body after the helper returns. `ret` returns from advance to its caller. It does not terminate the process. The register cards observe the state after the fragment reaches the supplied reporting code.
starter:
li a0, 9
li a1, 4
call advance
j entry_done
advance:
    addi a0, a0, 1
    add a0, a0, a1
    ret
entry_done:

prediction.prompt: What result is in a0 after advance returns and the fragment reaches entry_done?
prediction.hint: Apply both arithmetic instructions in the helper named advance. After ret, the caller’s jump skips the helper body.

explanation: The source label _start and the executable’s entry field serve related but different jobs. The label names code during assembly and linking. The ELF header tells xv6 the resulting start address. A file loader uses the executable’s loading information, not the visual position of the first interesting line in the editor.

xv6 is already running when it loads this user executable. It supplies the process’s address space and initial stack. This is not a firmware reset experiment, a board boot image or a direct write to a physical device. Those environments require their own startup and handoff contracts.

Changing the editor does not change an executable that was already built or a process that already ran. Build & Run creates and launches a fresh image. The source-change notice keeps that distinction visible when the displayed register snapshot belongs to an earlier version. Returning the correct value still matters independently of assembling and loading successfully.

experiment.task: Remove j entry_done immediately after call advance. Predict where ret sends control after the helper returns. Choose Start stepping and follow that return with Step instruction; use Stop to end the repeated path. Restore the jump afterwards.
experiment.hint: The call’s return address is the instruction immediately after the call. Check which instruction occupies that address after removing the jump.

challenge.task: Write a fragment that calls adjust, then skips its body. Pass t0, t1 and t2 into a0, a1 and a2 before the call. The helper must return a0 + a1 - a2 in a0. Keep ret inside the helper, not at the end of the top-level fragment.
challenge.starter:
mv a0, t0
mv a1, t1
mv a2, t2
call adjust
j entry_done
adjust:
    add a0, a0, a1
    ret
entry_done:
challenge.reference:
mv a0, t0
mv a1, t1
mv a2, t2
call adjust
j entry_done
adjust:
    add a0, a0, a1
    sub a0, a0, a2
    ret
entry_done:
hints: The first three incoming arguments use a0, a1 and a2.
The correction reduces the accumulated result; assembling successfully does not establish that calculation.
After ret, the caller must jump over the helper body before reaching the lab’s report.

originalityNote: The source course’s loader and startup lesson is rebuilt around the actual xv6 user ELF contract instead of presenting an Arm bare-metal startup as a RISC-V program.

title: Keep an access inside its permitted range
summary: Separate an application’s byte bounds from xv6’s process memory protection.
objectives: Check a byte offset before loading from a bounded record.
Distinguish a logical record boundary from an operating-system memory boundary.
before: A user process has an address space: the addresses xv6 allows it to use. A load from an unmapped or forbidden address can trap into the kernel, which can terminate the process. The CPU’s load instruction does not promise that every possible address is usable.

The starter reads one byte from the mapped data at lesson_data, then adjusts that value. After Build & Run, select Inspect registers to find the hexadecimal address in t0. Open Tools → Memory and choose After. Does the base address of the captured data match t0?

An application often has a smaller boundary than the mapped memory region. A three-byte sensor record may sit inside a much larger mapped page. Reading its fourth byte can violate the record’s contract without causing an operating-system fault. Your code must check the record’s capacity before it performs the load.
starter:
la t0, lesson_data
lbu t1, 0(t0)
addi t2, t1, 1

prediction.prompt: What is in t2 after the valid byte load and adjustment?
prediction.hint: t0 holds an address; lbu puts the byte at that address in t1. The following addi adjusts that loaded value.

explanation: A trap transfers control to the execution environment in response to an event such as an invalid memory access. It is not an ordinary function return. If your fragment faults before reporting, there may be no completed register snapshot. Open Tools → Output → xv6 serial log to read what happened.

The challenge supplies an unsigned offset and a capacity. The comparison must happen before the address is used for a byte load. Equality is already outside the allowed offset range: a capacity of three permits offsets zero, one and two. A zero capacity permits no reads at all.

Unsigned comparison matters for addresses and counts. A large bit pattern that has a negative signed reading is not a small valid offset. A bounds test, a valid mapping and the intended object’s lifetime answer different questions. None should be substituted for another just because one example happens to run without a fault.

experiment.task: Replace la t0, lesson_data with li t0, -1, then choose Build & Run. Open Tools → Output → xv6 serial log. Check whether the load faults before a register report is produced. Restore la t0, lesson_data afterwards.
experiment.hint: The changed bit pattern is not an address inside the supplied user data region. Do not expect a normal returned byte.

challenge.task: t0 is an unsigned byte offset and t1 is the record capacity, at most 64. Return the byte at that offset in t2 only when offset < capacity. Otherwise leave t2 as -1 and perform no load from the record.
challenge.starter:
la t3, lesson_data
add t3, t3, t0
lbu t2, 0(t3)
challenge.reference:
li t2, -1
bgeu t0, t1, guarded_done
la t3, lesson_data
add t3, t3, t0
lbu t2, 0(t3)
guarded_done:
hints: Choose the rejection result before testing the offset.
An offset equal to capacity is already beyond the record.
Branch around the load when the unsigned offset is outside the allowed range.

originalityNote: A safe byte read and a guard-before-load challenge retain the source course’s failure diagnosis while distinguishing xv6 page protection from application record bounds.

title: Write and run a complete assembly program
summary: Define the entry point, store your own data, call a helper, write to the console and exit.
objectives: Explain how a complete xv6 program starts, calls a helper and exits.
Build, debug and run a standalone assembly source file.
before: This editor contains a whole xv6 user program. The linker uses the global label `_start` as the entry point. The program defines its own message and explicitly exits.
Find `_start`, `announce` and `message`. Predict the console line, then choose Build & Run and look in Output. Open View complete program to compare the build source with the editor.
starter:
.section .rodata
message:
    .ascii "Trip ready\n"
.equ message_length, . - message

.text
.globl _start
_start:
    call announce

    li a0, 0
    li a7, 2
    ecall

announce:
    li a0, 1
    la a1, message
    li a2, message_length
    li a7, 16
    ecall
    ret
explanation: `.section .rodata` places the message bytes in a read-only section. `.ascii` stores the bytes, including the newline, without a terminator. At the end of the message, the assembler subtracts its start address from the current location (`.`) to compute the byte count.

`.text` switches to instructions. `call announce` saves the return address in `ra`. Inside the helper, `a0` selects standard output, `a1` holds the message address, `a2` holds its length and `a7` selects xv6 `write` (16). The kernel returns the number of bytes written in `a0` on success.

`ret` resumes after the call. Back in `_start`, the program sets `a0` to the exit status and `a7` to xv6 `exit` (2), then executes `ecall`. A process enters at `_start` and finishes through the exit syscall.

experiment.task: Change the message to a longer one and predict its new byte count. Set a breakpoint on the helper’s `ret` and choose Start debugging. Check `a0` in Registers for the number of bytes written. Step once to see control return to `_start`, then Continue and compare Output with your prediction.
experiment.hint: Count the newline as one byte for an ASCII message. The assembler recalculates `message_length` when you build.

independentTask: Download the worked source if you want to keep it. Clear the editor and write a new program that prints `Trip complete` followed by a newline. Put the string and its calculated length in read-only data, call your own printing helper from `_start`, and exit with status zero.

Build & Run. Check that Output contains exactly one line reading `Trip complete`. Set a breakpoint on the exit `ecall` and run again with Start debugging. Confirm that `a0` is zero and `a7` is two before you Continue.
Before marking this lesson complete, explain where the bytes are stored, where `ret` goes, and how xv6 knows to terminate the process. Download your program as a single assembly file.
originalityNote: The complete xv6 program combines the course’s entry, call and system-call mechanisms in a standalone console exercise.

title: Build a checked trip calculation
summary: Combine bounded records, status masks, a loop and a helper call in one executed program.
objectives: Integrate a record stride, a status test and a bounded accumulation.
Pass the accumulated value to a helper and inspect its returned result.
before: A trip record here occupies four bytes. Its first two bytes hold an unsigned distance in little-endian order. Byte two holds status bits, and byte three is reserved. The byte view marks each record’s start. The count in t0 says how many records to inspect, with a maximum of four.

The mask in t1 chooses the status bit or bits that make a record active. A record contributes when its status AND the mask is nonzero. The scale in t2 multiplies the final total. The supplied values keep every distance, sum and scaled result within the unsigned 64-bit range.

The fragment first walks the records and accumulates distances in a0. It then passes the scale in a1 and calls a leaf helper, a function that calls no other function. The helper returns the scaled total in a0. The snapshot is taken after that helper returns and the caller jumps past its body.
starter:
la t3, lesson_data
li t4, 0
li a0, 0
scan_records:
    bgeu t4, t0, scale_records
    lbu t5, 2(t3)
    and t5, t5, t1
    beqz t5, next_record
    lhu t6, 0(t3)
    add a0, a0, t6
next_record:
    addi t3, t3, 4
    addi t4, t4, 1
    j scan_records
scale_records:
    mv a1, t2
    call scale_total
    j trip_done
scale_total:
    mul a0, a0, a1
    ret
trip_done:

prediction.prompt: What scaled total is returned after only the first three records are considered?
prediction.hint: Consider only the records selected by the count. Include a distance when status AND mask is nonzero, then scale the accumulated total.

explanation: The count check precedes the read. For a zero count, the loop skips all record accesses and the zero total reaches the scaling helper. Otherwise the pointer advances by the full four-byte record size, not by the two-byte distance field or the one-byte status field.

A status byte is a bit pattern. Comparing it with the mask for equality would reject a record that has the desired bit plus another bit. AND tests the requested bits while allowing unrelated status bits. The branch decides whether to include the distance; it does not change the stored record.

The helper call separates accumulation from scaling. Its result contract is a0, so the caller uses that returned value rather than assuming an earlier temporary register still holds the answer. This program combines the mechanisms already taught, but one successful example is not enough evidence. Fresh cases include an empty list, different selected bits and a mask selecting nothing.

experiment.task: Add li t0, 4 before la t3, lesson_data. This replaces the supplied record count inside the fragment. Predict whether the fourth record contributes under the current mask. Choose Build & Run and compare a0 after the helper returns. Keep the data unchanged.
experiment.hint: First decide whether the fourth record is inspected; then test its status against the mask.

challenge.task: Using at most four records from lesson_data, sum each unsigned 16-bit distance whose status byte has any bit selected by t1. t0 supplies the record count and t2 the scale. Return total * scale in a0. Do not read a record after the count is exhausted. The cases keep the product within range.
challenge.reference:
la t3, lesson_data
li t4, 0
li a0, 0
scan_records:
    bgeu t4, t0, scale_records
    lbu t5, 2(t3)
    and t5, t5, t1
    beqz t5, next_record
    lhu t6, 0(t3)
    add a0, a0, t6
next_record:
    addi t3, t3, 4
    addi t4, t4, 1
    j scan_records
scale_records:
    mv a1, t2
    call scale_total
    j trip_done
scale_total:
    mul a0, a0, a1
    ret
trip_done:
hints: Use the count to guard each read, and advance by the four-byte record stride.
Test status AND mask for nonzero rather than testing status equal to mask.
Accumulate eligible distances first; pass the total and scale to the helper only after the loop ends.

originalityNote: The source course’s trip-computer quantities become an integrated RISC-V/xv6 record-processing program with independently varied count, status mask and scale.

title: Boot a bare-metal trip computer
summary: Boot your own assembly image in the browser, then run the same ELF on QEMU’s RISC-V virtual board.
objectives: Follow a bare-metal program from entry through stack setup, UART output and the final wait loop.
Transfer the same RISC-V ELF from the browser to QEMU and identify what depends on the board.
before: This trip computer is the first code the browser’s WebAssembly machine runs. The emulator loads the ELF and sets the program counter to its entry. Your code sets the stack pointer and uses a memory-mapped serial device (UART) to print its result.

Add the three distances in `distances` by hand. Choose Build & Run and check the total in UART output. Then choose Start stepping. At `_start`, find `sp` in Registers. Step through both machine instructions emitted by `la sp, __stack_top` and check where the stack pointer now points.
starter:
.option norvc
.equ UART_BASE, 0x10000000
.equ UART_STATUS, 5
.equ UART_TX_READY, 0x20

.section .text.boot, "ax"
.globl _start
_start:
    la sp, __stack_top
    la a0, heading
    call uart_puts

    la t0, distances
    la t1, distances_end
    li a0, 0
sum_distances:
    beq t0, t1, print_total
    lwu t2, 0(t0)
    add a0, a0, t2
    addi t0, t0, 4
    j sum_distances

print_total:
    call uart_number
    la a0, units
    call uart_puts

# The transmit buffer is empty on return. Leave the hart here.
.globl park
park:
    j park

.text
# a0 holds an unsigned total. Build decimal digits backwards on the stack.
uart_number:
    addi sp, sp, -32
    sd ra, 24(sp)
    addi t0, sp, 20
    sb zero, 0(t0)
    li t1, 10
decimal_digit:
    remu t2, a0, t1
    divu a0, a0, t1
    addi t2, t2, '0'
    addi t0, t0, -1
    sb t2, 0(t0)
    bne a0, zero, decimal_digit
    mv a0, t0
    call uart_puts
    ld ra, 24(sp)
    addi sp, sp, 32
    ret

# a0 points to a zero-terminated string. Access UART registers one byte at a time.
uart_puts:
    li t0, UART_BASE
next_byte:
    lbu t1, 0(a0)
    beq t1, zero, drain_uart
wait_for_uart:
    lbu t2, UART_STATUS(t0)
    andi t2, t2, UART_TX_READY
    beq t2, zero, wait_for_uart
    sb t1, 0(t0)
    addi a0, a0, 1
    j next_byte
drain_uart:
    lbu t2, UART_STATUS(t0)
    andi t2, t2, UART_TX_READY
    beq t2, zero, drain_uart
    ret

.section .rodata
heading:
    .asciz "Trip total: "
units:
    .asciz " km\r\n"
.balign 4
distances:
    .word 12, 7, 23
distances_end:
explanation: The linker script places startup at `0x80000000` and reserves stack space in RAM. The distances are 32-bit words, so the loop reads them with `lwu` and advances the address by four bytes. The decimal helper saves `ra` before calling the printing helper.

The UART starts at `0x10000000`. The printing loop reads the line status byte at offset 5. When bit 5 is set, it writes one byte to offset 0. After the last byte leaves the holding register, the program reaches `park`. The browser ends the run there. On a machine that keeps running, the final jump sends the hart back to `park` repeatedly.

experiment.task: Replace the three distances with four values that add up to more than 99. Predict the total, then check the UART line. Add a breakpoint on the call to `uart_number` and confirm that `a0` holds the total before the call.
experiment.hint: The loop stops when it reaches `distances_end`. Adding a word before that label makes it part of the calculation on the next build.

independentTask: Change the loop to count only readings of 10 km or more. Try 9, 10 and 11, then predict and verify the resulting total. The reading equal to 10 should count.
Keep that change for QEMU. Explain where the stack pointer comes from, why the UART status is polled, and where the program waits after printing.

bootTransfer.qemuIntro: Build your edited program and choose Download ELF. With QEMU’s RISC-V system emulator installed, run this command from the folder containing `trip.elf`.
bootTransfer.qemuCheck: Check that QEMU prints the same line as the browser. QEMU’s virtual reset code hands off to the image at `0x80000000`. The program then waits in `park`. To quit QEMU, press Ctrl+A and then x.
bootTransfer.board: Download the ready-to-run UF2 firmware and copy it to the Pico 2 in BOOTSEL mode. The starter firmware prints `Trip total: 42 km` over USB serial. If you want to try your own readings, edit the 32-bit RISC-V source and build a new UF2 in your browser using the guide.

originalityNote: The trip calculation becomes an original RV64 program with a startup routine, a linker script and a memory-mapped UART for the lab emulator and QEMU’s virt machine.

title: Derive fixed-width negation
summary: Use complement and addition to negate a 64-bit bit pattern.
objectives: Connect fixed-width negation with complement plus one.
Explain why the most-negative signed value has no positive partner at the same width.
before: Two’s complement assigns a signed reading to a fixed-width bit pattern. In a 64-bit value, the top bit has weight minus two to the power 63; the remaining bits keep their positive place values. The same stored pattern also has an unsigned reading. Choosing a reading does not alter the bits.

Complementing a pattern replaces every zero with one and every one with zero. The pseudo-instruction not performs that bitwise complement. The example then adds one. Keep only the low 64 bits, as the machine’s integer addition requires, and predict the signed reading of the resulting t2.

This rule describes fixed-width machine negation. It does not give C permission to overflow a signed type. The assembly example and its challenge operate on register bits directly; any related C expression still has to meet the C type’s own rules.
starter:
li t0, 5
not t1, t0
addi t2, t1, 1

prediction.prompt: What signed reading does t2 have after complementing the starting pattern and adding one?
prediction.hint: The complement in t1 is an intermediate value. Include the following addition before choosing the signed reading of t2.

explanation: For a 64-bit pattern x, complementing every bit gives the unsigned maximum minus x. Adding one therefore gives the low-bit representation of zero minus x. The modulo operation also explains why a carry out of the width is discarded rather than stored in an extra register bit.

Zero is a useful boundary: complementing it first produces all ones, and the following addition wraps back to zero. Two’s complement has one zero pattern. It also has one more negative signed value than positive values, so negating the most-negative value leaves the same stored pattern at this width.

experiment.task: Change li t0, 5 to li t0, 0 and run it. Then use li t0, 0x8000000000000000, the most-negative 64-bit pattern. Before each run, predict whether t2’s stored pattern will match t0. Compare their hexadecimal readings in Registers.
experiment.hint: Work modulo the fixed register width before choosing a signed reading. Hexadecimal compares the stored patterns directly.

challenge.task: Leave the low 64 bits of zero minus the incoming t0 pattern in t2. Use complement followed by addition. The challenge compares stored bit patterns, including the most-negative signed pattern.
challenge.reference:
not t2, t0
addi t2, t2, 1
hints: Bitwise complement alone is one short of the required fixed-width negation.
The addition must use the complemented value, not the original input.
Discard a carry beyond bit 63; there is no extra result bit in t2.

originalityNote: The source course’s fixed-width derivation is retained while the executed experiment uses full RV64 registers and distinguishes the miniature width from the machine width.

title: Moving from RISC-V to Arm
summary: Translate a function’s register roles and width, then run its Arm version in the other lab.
objectives: Identify architecture-specific state when translating assembly.
Choose an unsigned RISC-V branch from the required value relationship.
before: Different instruction sets can implement the same calculation without exposing the same intermediate state. Arm’s flag-setting additions can record condition bits such as carry. Base RISC-V integer addition writes a register result but has no Arm-style NZCV flags. This example makes the lost unsigned carry explicit in another register.

After add computes the low 64-bit sum in t2, sltu writes one to t3 when that sum is unsigned-smaller than the original first operand. The prediction concerns t3 after both instructions have run. It is a register containing a Boolean, not an architectural carry flag.

Width rules also differ. An Arm write through a 32-bit W name clears the upper half of the matching X register. An RV64 W-suffixed arithmetic instruction instead sign-extends its low 32-bit result to 64 bits. Renaming registers or instructions without checking that rule can change the values used by later comparisons.
starter:
li t0, -1
li t1, 1
add t2, t0, t1
sltu t3, t2, t0

prediction.prompt: What Boolean is in t3 after the explicit unsigned carry check?
prediction.hint: Compare the low 64-bit sum with the original first operand using unsigned ordering. sltu returns the truth of that comparison.

explanation: Translate the required relationship first. An unsigned maximum needs an unsigned ordering of the two stored patterns. RISC-V can express that choice with a direct branch such as bgeu; it does not need an instruction that reproduces an Arm compare’s flags before the branch.

Pseudo-instructions add another translation boundary. A source spelling such as li, call or ret can expand into one or more machine instructions. With compressed instructions enabled, decoded instruction widths can differ too. Do not carry across a rule that each source line or each instruction must advance the program counter by four bytes.

The environment remains a separate concern. Two machines may use RISC-V instructions while assigning different meanings to a system call number or a device address. Match the instruction set, width, calling convention and operating environment independently. A familiar mnemonic alone does not establish that a complete program can run unchanged.

experiment.task: Change li t0, -1 to li t0, 255. Keep the add and sltu instructions unchanged. Predict the unsigned carry check, then choose Build & Run and compare t3 in Registers.
experiment.hint: Crossing an eight-bit boundary is not a carry beyond a 64-bit register.

challenge.task: Return the larger of the incoming t0 and t1 patterns under unsigned 64-bit ordering, leaving the chosen pattern in t2. Use a direct RISC-V branch; do not use signed ordering when the top bit is set.
challenge.starter:
mv t2, t0
bge t0, t1, maximum_done
mv t2, t1
maximum_done:
challenge.reference:
mv t2, t0
bgeu t0, t1, maximum_done
mv t2, t1
maximum_done:
hints: The choice concerns unsigned magnitude, not the signed decimal display.
RISC-V branch operands are compared directly; there is no preceding cmp flag state to preserve.
The u in the branch spelling selects the unsigned relationship.

originalityNote: The optional cross-architecture comparison focuses on semantic differences that change a result, rather than presenting recorded Arm instructions as live RISC-V code.

title: Inspect a floating-point encoding as bits
summary: Extract fields from stored binary32 bytes using integer loads and shifts.
objectives: Separate a floating-point representation from an integer reading of the same bits.
Extract a binary32 field without claiming to execute floating-point instructions.
before: IEEE 754 binary32 stores a sign in bit 31, an exponent in bits 30 through 23, and a fraction in bits 22 through 0. The stored exponent controls a power-of-two scale. A value whose exponent field is neither all zeros nor all ones is called a normal value. Its fraction has an implied leading one.

The supplied four bytes encode 9.5 in binary32, in little-endian byte order. The live fragment uses lwu to load those bytes as an unsigned 32-bit bit pattern. It shifts away the fraction and masks the exponent field into t2. Predict that integer field, not a floating-point calculation.

This experiment executes integer RISC-V instructions only. The current xv6 guest does not provide the floating-point context used by a floating-point application. Reading an encoding as integer bits does not show that floating-point instructions, exception flags or a rounding mode are being exercised.
starter:
la t0, lesson_data
lwu t1, 0(t0)
srli t2, t1, 23
andi t2, t2, 255

prediction.prompt: What unsigned exponent field is extracted from the supplied binary32 encoding?
prediction.hint: Read the four bytes in little-endian order. The shift removes the fraction bits; the mask keeps only the exponent field.

explanation: For a normal binary32 value, subtract 127 from the stored exponent to obtain the power of two. That offset is called the exponent bias. The fraction field gives the bits after the implied leading one. Its weights are halves, quarters and further powers of one half. The encoding differs from a two’s-complement integer even when both occupy four bytes.

The normal rule has exceptions. An all-zero exponent with a zero fraction represents signed zero. With a nonzero fraction it represents a subnormal value, using a fixed small scale and no implied leading one. An all-one exponent represents infinity when the fraction is zero and NaN, “not a number”, when it is nonzero.

The sign bit belongs to the floating-point encoding. In particular, positive and negative zero have different stored sign bits. Loading binary32 bytes with lwu zero-extends them into a 64-bit integer register, so a signed comparison of that widened integer is not a way to recover the binary32 sign. Extract bit 31 instead.

experiment.task: After lwu t1, 0(t0), insert li t3, 0x80000000 and xor t1, t1, t3 before the shift. This changes only bit 31 of the loaded copy in t1; it leaves the supplied memory bytes unchanged. Predict whether the exponent in t2 changes, then choose Build & Run and compare t1 and t2 in Registers.
experiment.hint: XOR switches each bit selected by its mask. This mask selects the sign bit; the exponent occupies bits 30 through 23.

challenge.task: Load the first four bytes of lesson_data with lwu and leave their binary32 sign bit in t2 as 0 or 1. Do not classify the encoding with a signed integer comparison. Negative zero must retain its sign bit.
challenge.starter:
la t0, lesson_data
lwu t1, 0(t0)
slti t2, t1, 0
challenge.reference:
la t0, lesson_data
lwu t1, 0(t0)
srli t2, t1, 31
andi t2, t2, 1
hints: The floating-point sign is a field at a fixed bit position.
lwu clears the upper 32 bits, so the widened integer does not have a negative signed 64-bit reading.
Shift bit 31 into bit zero and keep that one bit.

originalityNote: The source course’s encoding distinction is retained as an integer-only memory experiment, with negative zero exposing why a widened signed-integer test is wrong.
